title: Limits and Continuity: The Gateway to Calculus

questions.question: Evaluate lim (x->2) of (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2).
questions.rationale: Factor the numerator: (x-2)(x+2)/(x-2) = x + 2 for all x near 2 (except at 2, which the limit ignores). The limit is 2 + 2 = 4 — a removable discontinuity lives at the point itself.

questions.question: lim (x->0) of sin(4x)/(7x) equals:
questions.rationale: Write sin(4x)/(7x) = [sin(4x)/(4x)] x (4/7). The bracket tends to 1 by the standard limit, so the answer is 4/7. The ratio of coefficients survives every time.

questions.question: The one-sided limits of |x|/x as x approaches 0 are:
questions.rationale: For x slightly negative, |x|/x = (-x)/x = -1; for x positive, |x|/x = x/x = 1. Since the left limit (-1) differs from the right limit (+1), the two-sided limit does not exist — a jump.

questions.question: For f(x) = (3x^2 + 2)/(5x^2 - 7), lim (x->infinity) equals:
questions.rationale: Divide numerator and denominator by x^2: all terms with x in the denominator vanish, leaving 3/5. With equal degrees the limit at infinity is the ratio of leading coefficients.

questions.question: lim (n->infinity) of (1 + 3/n)^(2n) equals:
questions.rationale: Rewrite as [(1 + 3/n)^(n/3)]^6. The inner bracket tends to e, so the whole limit is e^6. For 1^infinity forms, the exponent times the small quantity is the power of e.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three conditions for continuity of f at x = a?
options: The limit as x->a must exist
f must be differentiable at a
questions.rationale: Continuity demands definedness, an existing limit, and their equality — nothing about differentiability. Absolute value functions are continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at the kink.

questions.question: The function f(x) = 1/x at x = 0 has which kind of discontinuity?
questions.rationale: As x -> 0, 1/x blows up to plus or minus infinity on the two sides — an infinite discontinuity. No redefinition of f(0) can repair it, unlike a removable (hole) discontinuity.

questions.question: lim (x->0) of (e^(5x) - 1)/(3x) equals:
questions.rationale: Standard limit: (e^u - 1)/u -> 1. Write (e^(5x)-1)/(3x) = [(e^(5x)-1)/(5x)] x (5/3); the bracket tends to 1, giving 5/3 — the same coefficient trick as sin(kx)/(mx).

questions.question: By the Intermediate Value Theorem, if f is continuous on [1, 2] with f(1) = -3 and f(2) = 5, then:
options: f takes the value 0 somewhere in (1, 2)
questions.rationale: A continuous function on an interval takes every value between its endpoint values — including 0, since -3 and 5 straddle it. Note the theorem guarantees existence of a root, not monotonicity or a specific midpoint value.

questions.question: lim (x->a) of (x^5 - a^5)/(x - a) equals:
questions.rationale: Standard algebraic limit: (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) -> n a^(n-1). With n = 5 the answer is 5a^4 — the very formula that becomes the derivative of x^5 in the next chapter.
